topics.topic_name: Stimuli and Response in Living Organisms
concept_bullets: Living organisms sense and respond to environmental changes
Stimuli are detectable changes in external (temperature, light, sound) or internal (hunger, thirst, pain) environments
Response is the organism's functional reaction to a stimulus
Stimulus-response mechanism distinguishes living from non-living things

topics.modified_chunk: Living organisms sense environmental changes and respond accordingly. These detectable changes—external (temperature, light, sound) or internal (hunger, thirst, pain)—are stimuli. For example, you pull your hand from heat, plants bend toward sunlight, animals flee danger. The organism's functional reaction to a stimulus is called response. This mechanism distinguishes living from non-living things, enabling survival and adaptation.
topics.original_chunk: All living organisms can sense changes in their environment and respond to it accordingly. These changes are detectable in the external or internal environment of an organism and is called stimuli. The ability of an organism to react, due to stimulus, in the form of some functional action in the body is called response.

topics.topic_name: The Nervous System as a Control System
concept_bullets: The nervous system is a control system that monitors the environment and triggers responses
Receptors are specialized cells that detect stimuli (photoreceptors detect light, olfactory receptors detect smell, gustatory receptors detect taste)
Effectors are organs that produce responses (muscles contract for movement, glands secrete substances)
Information flow: Receptors detect → Nervous system processes → Effectors respond

topics.modified_chunk: The nervous system monitors your environment like a security system. Receptors are specialized sensor cells: photoreceptors in eyes detect light, olfactory receptors in nose detect smell, and gustatory receptors on tongue detect taste. When stimuli are detected, effectors respond—muscles contract (pulling hand from heat) and glands secrete substances (sweat when hot). Flow: Receptors detect → Nervous system processes → Effectors respond.
topics.original_chunk: The nervous system is a control system that enables humans to respond by receiving information from their surroundings through sense organs. Receptors detect different stimuli, e.g., photoreceptors in eye, smell receptors in nose, and taste receptors in tongue. Effectors bring about responses, e.g., muscles and glands.

concept_bullets: Axons transmit nerve impulses away from the cell body to target cells

topics.modified_chunk: Axons transmit nerve impulses away from the neuron's cell body toward other cells. At their endpoints, called axon terminals, axons form specialized junctions with target neurons, muscles, or glands. This junction, where nerve impulses pass from one neuron to another or to an effector organ, is called a synapse—the critical communication point in the nervous system.
topics.original_chunk: The axons transmit nerve impulses away from the cell body. The axon terminals form junctions with other neurons or with effector organs like muscles and glands. The junction between two neurons or between a neuron and an effector organ is called a synapse.

concept_bullets: Nerve cells (neurons) cannot divide or regenerate like other body cells

This unique property makes nervous system injuries particularly serious

topics.modified_chunk: Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells transmitting signals from the central nervous system to muscles and glands. They have three parts: cell body (controls activities), dendrites (receive signals), and axon (carries signals to muscles). Motor neurons have long axons reaching from spinal cord to distant body parts like fingers and toes. They control voluntary movements (writing, walking) and involuntary movements (reflexes). When your brain decides to move, electrical signals travel through motor neuron axons to muscles, causing contraction and enabling movement.
topics.original_chunk: Motor neurons transmit signals from the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) to muscles and glands. They have cell body, dendrites, and long axons. Motor neurons control voluntary movements like writing and walking, and involuntary movements like reflexes. Electrical signals travel down the axon to muscles, causing contraction and allowing movement to be initiated.

intro.title: Introduction
intro.description: Light travels in a straight line. This fundamental property of light helps us understand how we see objects and how light behaves in different situations.

matchbox_setup.title: Matchbox Setup
matchbox_setup.description: Take three matchboxes and make a small hole in each one. Align them so that the holes are in a straight line. This setup will help us observe how light travels.

matchbox_aligned.title: Aligned Matchboxes
matchbox_aligned.description: When the matchboxes are aligned in a straight line, light from a torch can pass through all three holes. This demonstrates that light travels in a straight line.

matchbox_misaligned.title: Misaligned Matchboxes
matchbox_misaligned.description: When one matchbox is moved out of alignment, light cannot pass through all the holes. This confirms that light travels only in straight lines and cannot bend around obstacles.

pipe_intro.title: Pipe Introduction
pipe_intro.description: Another way to observe light traveling in a straight line is by using a pipe. Let's see what happens when we shine light through different pipe configurations.

pipe_straight.title: Straight Pipe
pipe_straight.description: When light is shone through a straight pipe, it passes through easily. You can see the light at the other end, confirming that light travels in a straight line.

pipe_bent.title: Bent Pipe
pipe_bent.description: When the pipe is bent, light cannot pass through. This is because light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around corners. This is why we need mirrors or other reflective surfaces to change the direction of light.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.description: Through these experiments, we have learned that light always travels in a straight line. This property is fundamental to understanding how we see objects, how shadows are formed, and how optical devices work.
